lesson.title: Frühstück: das Frühstück, das Brötchen, die Marmelade, der Toast, die Butter
lesson.subtitle: the one meal with its own noun — and butter coming back as a compound

hook.title: Two Languages, Two Recipes for One Meal
hook.content: English and German built their breakfast word at home, from different parts. English breakfast is break + fast — the meal named for the fast it ends. das Frühstück is früh + Stück — 'early piece' — the first piece of bread taken early in the day, which is exactly what a breakfast roll still is. Same meal, two descriptions: English names what the meal ends, German names when you eat it. das Brötchen is Brot with the diminutive -chen — the little bread — the same job English does with -let (booklet), and German -chen is a true cousin of English -kin (lambkin). die Marmelade came from Portuguese marmelo, 'quince', and the quince's own name is Greek melímēlon — 'honey-apple' — so there is honey hiding in every jar of jam. der Toast is English toast, from Latin tostare, 'to scorch': English kept the Latin roast-word, and German borrowed it back from English. And the payoff is a compound you can already read: das Butterbrot — butter + Brot — the word for what English calls a sandwich, built out of two words you have owned since lesson 101.

footnotes.title: -chen Makes Everything das
footnotes.content: The diminutive -chen always makes the noun neuter: der Baum becomes das Bäumchen, die Katze becomes das Kätzchen, and das Brot stays das as das Brötchen. No exceptions, no memorizing — the suffix decides. That is why the little bread is das Brötchen even though bread rolls come in dozens.

pattern.title: Breakfast in Sentences
pattern.content: Four frames, one table. 1. Duration: Das Frühstück dauert zwanzig Minuten — dauern measures the meal in bare accusative time, no preposition, the lesson 5151 frame. 2. Frequency: Einmal in der Woche essen wir Toast — einmal + in + dative is the once-a-week frame, and the toast stands bare. 3. The table: Ich esse Brötchen mit Marmelade, Wir essen Brot mit Butter — mit + dative carries whatever rides along. 4. Taking it with you: Ich nehme ein Butterbrot mit — the separable particle mit drops to the end of the sentence, the same move as Ich stehe früh auf.
pattern.linguist_note: Breakfast is the rare meal the two languages name differently at the root: German records the early piece of bread a farmer ate before work; English records the monastic act of ending a night's fast. English 'dinner' grew from the same idea — Vulgar Latin disjeiunare, 'to break the fast' — before the main meal slid to midday. German stayed literal: früh + Stück, early + piece.

exercises.prompt: The breakfast table — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: Once a week we eat toast
matching_pairs.german: Einmal in der Woche essen wir Toast

matching_pairs.english: I take a sandwich with me
The sandwich with meat and cheese
matching_pairs.german: Das Butterbrot mit Fleisch und Käse

matching_pairs.english: We eat the roll without fork and knife
matching_pairs.german: Wir essen das Brötchen ohne Gabel und Messer

matching_pairs.english: A bottle of water for breakfast
The roll comes out of the oven
matching_pairs.german: Das Brötchen kommt aus dem Ofen

exercises.target_answer: Das Frühstück dauert zwanzig Minuten, Einmal in der Woche essen wir Toast, Ich esse Brötchen mit Marmelade, Wir essen Brot mit Butter, Ich nehme ein Butterbrot mit, Das Butterbrot mit Fleisch und Käse, Wir essen das Brötchen ohne Gabel und Messer, Seife vor dem Essen, Gemüse und Obst zum Frühstück, Honig auf dem Brötchen, Eine Flasche Wasser zum Frühstück, Das Brötchen kommt aus dem Ofen
exercises.meaning: breakfast duration, weekly toast, rolls with jam, bread and butter, a sandwich to go
exercises.explanation: dauern measures how long the meal takes — das Frühstück dauert zwanzig Minuten, bare accusative, no preposition. einmal in der Woche is the once-a-week frame, and mit carries what rides along: jam, butter, or the Butterbrot itself.

exercises.prompt: Which word wears the diminutive -chen — the suffix that always makes the noun das?
exercises.meaning: das Brötchen = Brot + -chen, the little bread
exercises.explanation: Brot + -chen = the little bread, neuter by rule — -chen makes every noun das, the same job English does with -let. Butterbrot is a plain compound (butter + Brot), while Marmelade and Toast are travelers from Portuguese and English.

Marmelade traveled from Portuguese marmelo (quince) — Greek melímēlon, 'honey-apple', hides inside. The honey itself German owns as Honig, lesson 5231's pure twin. On your Toast: Butter und Marmelade.

exercises.target_answer: Das Frühstück ist um sieben Uhr
exercises.explanation: um + the clock time — the frame from the first lessons, now serving a meal. das Frühstück is neuter twice over: built on das Stück, and it is the early piece itself.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'I eat toast with butter and jam'
exercises.target_answer: Ich esse Toast mit Butter und Marmelade
exercises.meaning: I eat toast with butter and jam
exercises.explanation: Three breakfast nouns, one mit, verb in slot 2. And the compound is waiting: butter + Brot = das Butterbrot — German can say this whole plate in one word.

summary.outcome: Talk about the one meal with its own noun: measure it with dauern, time it with um, and build the -chen and Butter- compounds yourself.

use_example.german: Das Frühstück dauert zwanzig Minuten — Brot mit Butter und Marmelade.
use_example.english: Breakfast lasts twenty minutes — bread with butter and jam.

summary.takeaway: Frühstück is früh + Stück, 'early piece' (English named the broken fast instead), Brötchen is the -chen little bread, Marmelade hides Greek honey, Toast is English's Latin — and Butterbrot is butter + Brot, both lesson-101 words.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Farben I — rot, blau, grün, schwarz, bunt, where German hardens red's d into rot's t.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Frühstück: das Frühstück, das Brötchen, die Marmelade, der Toast, die Butter (I eat toast with butter and jam):
twist.target_answer: Ich esse Toast mit Butter und Marmelade
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Ich esse Toast mit Butter und Marmelade" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Frühstück: das Frühstück, das Brötchen, die Marmelade, der Toast, die Butter without relying on short-term echo.

frühstück.context_phrase: Das Frühstück ist um sieben Uhr.
frühstück.etymology_derivation: Literally 'early piece (bite)': früh + Stück; NOT the break-fast calque English uses. [wiktionary]

brötchen.context_phrase: Ich kaufe jeden Morgen frische Brötchen.
brötchen.context_translation: I buy fresh rolls every morning.
brötchen.etymology_derivation: Brötchen — diminutive of Brot (bread), which is cognate with English bread; both trace to PIE *bʰrewh₁-, the root of brew. [wiktionary]

marmelade.etymology_derivation: Marmelade — 16th century, from Middle French marmelade, from Portuguese marmelada (quince jam); English marmalade took the same route. [wiktionary]

toast.etymology_derivation: Toast — borrowed straight from English toast, with toasten and Toaster as later German offshoots. [wiktionary]

butterbrot.context_phrase: Ich nehme ein Butterbrot mit in die Schule.
butterbrot.context_translation: I take a sandwich to school.
butterbrot.etymology_derivation: Butter + Brot — both elements are documented twins (Butter via Latin butyrum, Brot kin to brew); an exact internal calque. [wiktionary]

butter.etymology_derivation: Borrowed together into West Germanic from Latin butyrum / Greek boutyron.

einmal.context_phrase: Einmal im Jahr fahre ich ans Meer.
einmal.context_translation: Once a year I go to the sea.
einmal.etymology_derivation: ein 'one' + Mal 'time': Middle High German einmāle — literally one-time, hence once. [wiktionary]

dauern.etymology_derivation: From Latin dūrō via Middle Low German — kin to archaic English dure, as in endure. [wiktionary]

fleisch.context_phrase: Ich esse gern Fleisch mit Kartoffeln.
fleisch.context_translation: I like eating meat with potatoes.
fleisch.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *flaiski — the exact counterpart of English flesh. [wiktionary]

käse.context_phrase: Der Käse auf dem Brot ist lecker.
käse.context_translation: The cheese on the bread is tasty.
käse.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *kāsī, borrowed early from Latin cāseus — shared with English cheese. [wiktionary]

gabel.context_phrase: Ich esse den Salat mit der Gabel.
gabel.context_translation: I am eating the salad with the fork.
gabel.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic gabulu, meaning fork; English gable is the same Germanic word, naming the fork-shaped upper end of a house wall. [wiktionary]

messer.context_phrase: Schneide das Brot mit dem Messer.
messer.context_translation: Cut the bread with the knife.
messer.etymology_derivation: From Old High German mezzisahs, literally food knife; the first part is the food root behind English meat, the second the knife root behind English saw, with t appearing as ss in German. [wiktionary]

becher.context_phrase: Ich trinke den Kakao aus einem Becher.
becher.context_translation: I am drinking the cocoa from a mug.
becher.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic bikari, borrowed from Latin bicarium, likely a diminutive of Greek bikos, meaning jar or amphora; English beaker is the same Latin loan. [wiktionary]

kanne.context_phrase: Die Kanne Tee ist noch heiß.
kanne.context_translation: The pot of tea is still hot.
kanne.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic kanno; English can is a direct cognate from Old English canne, originally meaning cup or vessel. [wiktionary]

flasche.context_phrase: Die Flasche Wasser kostet zwei Euro.
flasche.context_translation: The bottle of water costs two euros.
flasche.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic flasko, from a root meaning to plait or braid, since bottles were once wrapped in straw; English flask is a direct cognate. [wiktionary]

ofen.context_phrase: Der Kuchen ist noch im Ofen.
ofen.context_translation: The cake is still in the oven.
ofen.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic ofn; English oven is a direct cognate from the same Germanic word, differing only in the vowel. [wiktionary]

gemüse.etymology_derivation: From Old High German muos 'food, porridge'; English mush is only a possible cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

herd.context_phrase: Der Topf steht auf dem Herd.
herd.context_translation: The pot is on the stove.
herd.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic herth; English hearth is a direct cognate, the English th corresponding to German d. [wiktionary]

seife.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic saipo, from the PIE root seyb, meaning to pour or trickle; English soap is a direct cognate, its p corresponding to German f after the High German shift. [wiktionary]

zucker.context_phrase: Ich nehme Zucker in den Kaffee.
zucker.context_translation: I take sugar in my coffee.
zucker.etymology_derivation: Via Italian zucchero from Arabic sukkar, Sanskrit śárkarā — the same trade-route loan as English sugar. [wiktionary]

suppe.etymology_derivation: Borrowed via Middle Low German suppe under French influence — both trace to Proto-Germanic *supô 'broth'. [wiktionary]

obst.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *obaet; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

tomate.context_phrase: Die Tomate ist rot und reif.
tomate.context_translation: The tomato is red and ripe.
tomate.etymology_derivation: From Spanish/French tomate, Classical Nahuatl tomatl — the same New World loan as English tomato. [wiktionary]

honig.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *hunag — Wiktionary: 'Cognate with English honey'. [wiktionary]

keks.context_phrase: Ich nehme einen Keks zum Kaffee.
keks.context_translation: I am taking a cookie with my coffee.
keks.etymology_derivation: Keks — a 1900s borrowing of English cakes, popularized when Bahlsen renamed Leibniz-Cakes to Leibniz-Keks in 1911; northern German uses der, the south often das. [wiktionary]

torte.context_phrase: Zum Geburtstag backen wir eine Torte.
torte.context_translation: We are baking a cake for the birthday.
torte.etymology_derivation: Torte — 15th century, from Middle French tarte and tourte, later reinforced by Italian torta, from Late Latin torta (round loaf); English torte was borrowed back from German. [wiktionary]

schokolade.context_phrase: Die Schokolade ist für die Kinder.
schokolade.context_translation: The chocolate is for the children.
schokolade.etymology_derivation: Schokolade — borrowed via Dutch chocolade from Spanish chocolate, from Classical Nahuatl chocolātl; English chocolate comes from the same Spanish word. [wiktionary]

essen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + Ablaut Vowels
essen.context_translation: What do we want to eat?
essen.etymology_derivation: Medial t → ss. Noun: das Essen (food).

brot.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *braudą — originally "the fermented/risen thing", kin to the verb brew (German brauen). Bread is "the brewed thing". [wiktionary]

minute.etymology_derivation: Medieval Latin minūta — the same Latin loan as English minute. [wiktionary]

uhr.etymology_derivation: Loan-cognate of hour (Latin hōra via French), and a distant doublet of Jahr and year (PIE *yóh₁r̥). German alone turned it into the word for the clock itself. [wiktionary]

woche.context_phrase: Nächste Woche fahre ich nach Berlin.
woche.context_translation: Next week I travel to Berlin.

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
